subject: Follow-up: logging obfuscation & trace header handling (Finexa)
messages:
From: Soojin Lee <soojin_lee@redwood.com>

Cc: Grace O'Connor <grace_oconnor@redwood.com>

Subject: Follow-up: logging obfuscation & trace header handling (Finexa)

Hi Elena / Jake — thanks again for the call today. Quick recap and proposed next steps so we have a single source of truth.

Summary of Finexa requirements we captured: 
- You need request + response logging for operational troubleshooting and latency investigations, but all PII needs to be removed from logs (names, SSNs, account numbers).
- Trace headers (X-Trace-Id and X-Request-Id) are used by Finexa for cross-service correlation; you want to preserve the ability to tie logs together but not exfiltrate raw trace IDs to Redwood storage.
- Log retention: 30 days for request/response logs; separate audit trail retained 12 months.
- Data residency: logs must reside in us-east-1 and not traverse EU/APAC storage.
- Compliance: you will require SOC2 evidence for log handling and an artifact showing our redaction logic.

Initial technical asks we heard: 
1) Mask or obfuscate trace IDs in stored logs but keep a mechanism to correlate within Finexa (deterministic hashing or tokenization).
2) Provide configurable redaction rules (regex + structured-field masking) that can run at the edge (ingest) or at the storage layer.
3) Low-latency path must remain within SLOs; any heavy post-processing should be asynchronous.

Proposed immediate next steps (from Redwood):
- We'll share a short design proposal that outlines edge scrubbing vs. server-side redaction and the tradeoffs for latency and throughput (attached: redaction-proposal-v1.pdf).
- Engineering demo of the redaction controls + runbook showing how trace IDs are handled. Suggested demo window: week of Sep 21.
- Finish a mutual action plan (MAP) with dates and ownership; I'll draft the MAP and share by Sep 16.
- Share a small sample transformation snippet (example config) that shows deterministic hashing of trace IDs and a sample hashed output on the example header you shared.

Questions for you that will help our engineering recommendation:
- Do you require the original trace ID value to be available to Finexa engineers (via a secure retrieval process) or do you only need stable mapped IDs for correlation?
- Is there an internal minimum entropy requirement on hashed values to avoid collisions?

If you confirm the demo window above and the two questions, we'll proceed to produce the MAP and the sample configs.

Best,
Soojin

Subject: Re: Follow-up: logging obfuscation & trace header handling (Finexa)

Thanks Soojin — that recap is great and aligned with what we discussed. A couple clarifications from the security side: 

1) We prefer not to ever store the raw trace IDs in Redwood-managed storage. Finexa engineers need correlation but we can accept a stable, reversible token only if it is stored in our vault (we'd rather avoid reversible storage in Redwood). So deterministic one-way hashing (with a per-customer salt managed by Finexa) would be our preference.
2) For troubleshooting, sometimes we need to re-link a raw trace to internal telemetry. If hashing is one-way, we need a secure process to submit a raw trace ID and get a matching hashed token back without exposing it in logs. Can Redwood support an API that accepts a trace ID and returns the hashed token (with mutual TLS / IP allowlist)?
3) Small sample header attached — our trace IDs today are 128-bit UUIDs in hex, e.g. 4a7d8f2b-... Illustrated in finexa-header-sample.png.

We can do the demo week of Sep 21; prefer Sep 22 afternoon PST. The MAP draft by Sep 16 works for us.

Also, one ask on retention: the 30-day window is our requirement for request logs, but audit logs (policy changes, redaction rule updates) must be immutable and available for 12 months for compliance review.

Thanks — Elena
Elena Rossi
Head of Platform Security | Finexa
elena@finexa.com
From: Sergio Alvarez <sergio_alvarez@redwood.com>

Subject: Re: Follow-up: logging obfuscation & trace header handling (Finexa)

On internal technical approach — notes for the MAP and demo: 

1) Edge scrubbing vs. server-side: 
- Edge scrubbing (ingest): run redaction and deterministic hashing at the edge ingress point. Pros: raw PII never lands in our central logs; simpler for compliance. Cons: more CPU at edge, potential added latency ~5-15ms per request depending on batching.
- Server-side post-processing: accept full log, then run async jobs to redact + hash. Pros: lower tail-latency for real-time requests; Cons: raw data touches central storage briefly — a compliance concern for Finexa.

2) Trace ID hashing design:
- We can implement a per-customer salt + HMAC-SHA256 truncated to 64 bits (hex) to keep the hashed id short while maintaining low collision risk. This is deterministic and non-reversible without the salt.
- Support an admin API (mutual-TLS + allowlist) that allows Finexa to submit the raw trace and receive the hashed token. We will not persist the raw trace on our side if the request is made to the retrieval endpoint; for auditing we would log the admin API call metadata (who, when) — those audit entries will live in the 12-month immutable store.

3) Configurable redaction rules: regex + structured JSON field masks. We have an example DSL we can expose in the demo.

4) Performance: need to warn Finexa about throughput impact for very high qps. We'll provide a benchmark with their expected peak qps in the MAP.

I'll include a short pros/cons appendix and a sample HMAC snippet for the MAP. Grace — can you validate the proposed retention and audit-store flows before I add them to the draft?

Thanks,
Sergio
